title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: Q5. Do Roads and Canals Explain Where Fires Burn?
text:
Q5. Do Roads and Canals Explain Where Fires Burn?






NoteShort answer



Only partly. Fires burned within reach of roads and tracks, and just 4 of 3,065 fire-days were more than 14 km from one. But a model built on distance to roads, canals and rivers removes little of the clustering, so access is not the main reason fires group together.




Question

Are fires closer to roads and canals, and does this explain the clustering?

Why ask

Most peat fires are started by people (Page and Hooijer, 2016), who reach the peat by road and canal. Canals also dry the peat out.

Method

Distance maps are built from OSM. rhohat() shows how fire intensity changes with each distance. ppm() then fits a Poisson point process model, a kind of regression for points, using the three distances.

Compared with what

The fitted access model replaces the KDE as the null in an inhomogeneous L test, to see how much clustering is left once access is allowed for.




Preparing the OSM Layers
Only OSM features within 5 km of the regency are read, so fires near the boundary can still see canals just outside.



read OSM waterways and roads near Pulang Pisau

pp_buf  <- st_buffer(pp_sf, 5000)
bbox_wkt <- st_as_text(st_geometry(st_transform(pp_buf, 4326)))

waterways <- st_read("data/rawdata/osm/gis_osm_waterways_free_1.shp",
                     wkt_filter = bbox_wkt, quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(32749) %>% st_intersection(pp_buf)
roads <- st_read("data/rawdata/osm/gis_osm_roads_free_1.shp",
                 wkt_filter = bbox_wkt, quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(32749) %>% st_intersection(pp_buf)

bind_rows(waterways %>% mutate(layer = "waterways"), roads %>% mutate(layer = "roads")) %>%
  mutate(km = as.numeric(st_length(geometry)) / 1000) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(used_as = case_when(fclass %in% c("canal", "drain") ~ "Canal",
                             fclass == "river" ~ "River",
                             layer == "roads" & !fclass %in% c("footway", "steps", "pedestrian") ~ "Road or track",
                             TRUE ~ "Not used")) %>%
  group_by(used_as) %>%
  summarise(types = paste(unique(fclass[order(-km)])[1:min(4, n_distinct(fclass))], collapse = ", "),
            features = n(), km = round(sum(km)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(km)) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Used as", "Main OSM types", "Features", "Length (km)"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

Canals are OSM canals and drains. Roads include all roads, tracks and paths except footways. Rivers are a control, because deep peat domes form between rivers.



distance surfaces in km

to_psp <- function(x) {
  g <- st_geometry(st_cast(st_cast(x, "MULTILINESTRING"), "LINESTRING"))
  rescale.psp(as.psp(g, W = as.owin(pp_buf)), 1000, "km")
}
canal_psp <- to_psp(filter(waterways, fclass %in% c("canal", "drain")))
river_psp <- to_psp(filter(waterways, fclass == "river"))
road_psp  <- to_psp(filter(roads, !fclass %in% c("footway", "steps", "pedestrian")))

grid <- as.mask(pp_owin_km, dimyx = c(400, 200))
covs <- list(d_canal = distmap(canal_psp, xy = grid),
             d_road  = distmap(road_psp,  xy = grid),
             d_river = distmap(river_psp, xy = grid))




How Fire Intensity Changes with Distance

The PlotThe Code










Figure 12. Fire intensity as a function of distance, rhohat estimates with 95% bands. Each x axis stops at the 98th percentile of distances in the regency. Data from NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and OpenStreetMap








rho_df <- imap_dfr(covs, function(im, nm) {
  d <- as.data.frame(rhohat(fire_ppp_u, im)) %>% rename(X = 1)
  cap <- quantile(im[pp_owin_km, drop = TRUE], 0.98, na.rm = TRUE)
  d %>% filter(X <= cap) %>% mutate(covariate = nm)
}) %>%
  mutate(covariate = recode(covariate, d_canal = "Distance to canal or drain",
                            d_road = "Distance to road or track",
                            d_river = "Distance to river"),
         covariate = factor(covariate, levels = c("Distance to road or track",
                            "Distance to canal or drain", "Distance to river")))
avg_int <- intensity(fire_ppp_u)

ggplot(rho_df, aes(X, rho)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = col_band, alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_line(colour = col_fire, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = avg_int, colour = col_accent, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ covariate, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Almost no fire burned more than 14 km from a road or track",
       subtitle = "Dashed blue line is the regency-wide average intensity",
       x = "Distance (km)", y = "Fire-days per km²") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())




Almost all fires were within reach of a road or track. Intensity stays near or above average up to about 12 km from one, then drops to almost zero. Only 4 of 3,065 fire-days were more than 14 km away, although that land is 16 percent of the regency. 82 percent of fire-days were within 5 km of a road or canal, against 65 percent of the land.
Intensity rises far from rivers, which fits peat domes. The canal curve is noisy, with peaks 50 to 60 km from any mapped canal in the northern strip, where OSM shows almost no canals. The curves show where fires burned, not why.


Fitting the Access Model

env_access <- envelope(fire_ppp_u, Linhom, simulate = sims_access, nsim = 99,

The access model fits much better than constant intensity, and its AIC (lower is better) falls from 13,220 to 12,511. But at 5 km, L(r) minus r only drops from 5.8 km under CSR to 5.34 km, against 3.55 km for the KDE null. The observed curve stays far above the access model’s envelope at all distances.
Fires are most common near roads and canals, but access explains little of why they cluster. Most of the clustering must come from things OSM does not hold, such as peat depth, land clearing or fires affecting each other. The model’s z values also look more certain than they are, because they ignore clustering.

title: Take-home Exercise 1
section: Q6. Do Recent Fires Predict New Ones Better Than a Hotspot Map?
text:
Q6. Do Recent Fires Predict New Ones Better Than a Hotspot Map?






NoteShort answer



Yes, on this season’s data. A zone within 3 km of the last three days’ fires caught 76 percent of newly burning cells on 15 percent of the land. A hotspot map of the same size caught at most 64 percent. The zone still needs testing on another year.




Question

Each morning a crew can watch only part of the regency. Should it watch near recent fires, or the places that have burned most?

Why ask

Q4 found that fires close in space were also close in time. Crime analysts call this a near-repeat pattern (Townsley et al., 2003). It is only useful if recent fires point to new fires better than a hotspot map does.

Compared with what

A hotspot zone of exactly the same size each day, and a zone that ignores fire history.



How the test works. It runs for every day from 4 July to 22 September.

The watch zone is the area within 3 km of the previous three days’ fires. The 3 km and 3 days come from Figure 11, so this is an in-sample test and may flatter the zone.
The hotspot zone covers the same amount of land on the highest part of a KDE of all earlier fires, at 1.5, 3 and 6 km bandwidths.
The target is newly burning cells, with no fire in the past 7 days.
A stricter target, separate new fires, has no other event within 2 km in the past 7 days.
Fires outside the regency are not used, which affects both zones equally.

A zone that ignored fire history would catch new cells in line with its share of land, which is the minimum to beat.



back-test the watch zone against same-size hotspot zones

fires <- fires %>%
  arrange(cell, date_local) %>%
  group_by(cell) %>%
  mutate(is_new = is.na(lag(date_local)) | as.numeric(date_local - lag(date_local)) > 7) %>%
  ungroup()

pp_area <- as.numeric(st_area(pp_sf))
grid_m  <- as.mask(pp_owin, eps = 500)   # 500 m pixels, in metres

hotspot_catch <- function(d, land, today, sigma) {
  past <- filter(fires, date_local <= d - 1)
  kd <- density(as.ppp(st_geometry(past), W = pp_owin), sigma = sigma, xy = grid_m, edge = TRUE)
  cut_value <- quantile(kd$v, 1 - land, na.rm = TRUE)   # same land share as the watch zone
  xy <- st_coordinates(today)
  sum(kd[ppp(xy[, 1], xy[, 2], window = pp_owin, check = FALSE)] >= cut_value, na.rm = TRUE)
}

watch <- map_dfr(seq(as_date("2026-07-04"), as_date("2026-09-22"), by = "day"), function(d) {
  recent <- filter(fires, date_local >= d - 3, date_local <= d - 1)
  today  <- filter(fires, date_local == d, is_new)
  if (nrow(recent) == 0 || nrow(today) == 0) {
    return(tibble(date = d, new = nrow(today), caught = 0, land = 0,
                  hot_1.5 = 0, hot_3 = 0, hot_6 = 0))
  }
  zone <- st_union(st_buffer(st_geometry(recent), 3000)) %>% st_intersection(st_geometry(pp_sf))
  land <- as.numeric(st_area(zone)) / pp_area
  tibble(date = d, new = nrow(today),
         caught  = sum(lengths(st_intersects(today, zone)) > 0),
         land    = land,
         hot_1.5 = hotspot_catch(d, land, today, 1500),
         hot_3   = hotspot_catch(d, land, today, 3000),
         hot_6   = hotspot_catch(d, land, today, 6000))
})

watch_sum <- watch %>%
  summarise(land_covered = weighted.mean(land, new),
            newly_burning = sum(new),
            watch_zone = sum(caught) / newly_burning,
            hotspot_1.5km = sum(hot_1.5) / newly_burning,
            hotspot_3km = sum(hot_3) / newly_burning,
            hotspot_6km = sum(hot_6) / newly_burning)


The next chunk gives a 95 percent interval for the gap, resampling whole weeks because nearby days share fires, and repeats the test for separate new fires.



uncertainty on the gap, and the stricter target

fire_days <- filter(watch, new > 0)
set.seed(2026)
fire_days$wk <- floor_date(fire_days$date, "week", week_start = 1)
weeks <- split(seq_len(nrow(fire_days)), fire_days$wk)
gap_boot <- replicate(999, {
  i <- unlist(sample(weeks, length(weeks), replace = TRUE))   # resample whole weeks
  (sum(fire_days$caught[i]) - sum(fire_days$hot_1.5[i])) / sum(fire_days$new[i])
})
days_better <- sum(fire_days$caught > fire_days$hot_1.5)
days_worse  <- sum(fire_days$caught < fire_days$hot_1.5)
gap_test <- tibble(
  gap_points = round(100 * (sum(fire_days$caught) - sum(fire_days$hot_1.5)) / sum(fire_days$new), 1),
  ci_low  = round(100 * quantile(gap_boot, 0.025), 1),
  ci_high = round(100 * quantile(gap_boot, 0.975), 1),
  days_watch_better = days_better, days_hotspot_better = days_worse,
  sign_test_p = signif(binom.test(days_better, days_better + days_worse)$p.value, 2))

# separate new fires, no other event within 2 km in the previous 7 days
fxy <- st_coordinates(fires)
fdd <- as.numeric(fires$date_local)
fires$separate_new <- map_lgl(seq_len(nrow(fires)), function(i) {
  near <- sqrt((fxy[, 1] - fxy[i, 1])^2 + (fxy[, 2] - fxy[i, 2])^2) <= 2000
  lag  <- fdd[i] - fdd
  !any(near & lag >= 1 & lag <= 7)
})

watch_strict <- map_dfr(seq(as_date("2026-07-04"), as_date("2026-09-22"), by = "day"), function(d) {
  recent <- filter(fires, date_local >= d - 3, date_local <= d - 1)
  today  <- filter(fires, date_local == d, separate_new)
  if (nrow(recent) == 0 || nrow(today) == 0) return(tibble(new = nrow(today), caught = 0, land = 0, hot = 0))
  zone <- st_union(st_buffer(st_geometry(recent), 3000)) %>% st_intersection(st_geometry(pp_sf))
  land <- as.numeric(st_area(zone)) / pp_area
  tibble(new = nrow(today), caught = sum(lengths(st_intersects(today, zone)) > 0),
         land = land, hot = hotspot_catch(d, land, today, 1500))
})

strict_sum <- watch_strict %>%
  summarise(land_covered = weighted.mean(land, new), separate_new_fires = sum(new),
            watch_zone = sum(caught) / separate_new_fires,
            hotspot_1.5km = sum(hot) / separate_new_fires)






Table 4. Share of new fires each zone caught, 4 Jul to 22 Sep 2026. Each hotspot zone covers the same land as that day’s watch zone

The chance row is the zone’s average share of the regency. The test starts on 4 July and covers 1,651 newly burning cells (2 fewer than the season total).

The PlotThe Code










Figure 13. Left, the watch zone on 18 September. Right, weekly share of newly burning cells caught. Weeks with fewer than 15 are left blank, and the last week holds only 21 and 22 September. Data from NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1








map_ex <- tm_shape(pp_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = col_land, col = "grey50") +
  tm_shape(ex_zone) +
  tm_polygons(fill = col_band, fill_alpha = 0.45, col = col_band) +
  tm_shape(ex_new) +
  tm_dots(fill = "where", size = 0.3,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("inside the zone" = col_fire,
                                                       "outside the zone" = col_accent)),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Newly burning, 18 Sep", text.size = 1, title.size = 1.1,
                                  position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom"))) +
  tm_scalebar(position = tm_pos_out("center", "bottom"), breaks = c(0, 20))

watch_lab <- watch_week %>%
  filter(!is.na(share)) %>%
  group_by(measure) %>%
  slice_max(week, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(label = c("Watch zone", "Hotspot zone,\nsame area", "Share of land\nin the zone")[as.integer(measure)])

chart <- ggplot(watch_week, aes(week, share, colour = measure, linetype = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_text(data = watch_lab, aes(label = label), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 2.5,
            size = 3.7, lineheight = 0.9, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_fire, "grey35", col_accent), guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "dashed"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%d %b", breaks = as_date(c("2026-07-01", "2026-08-01", "2026-09-01")),
               expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.28))) +
  labs(title = paste0("Recent fires beat a same-size hotspot map in ", wk_won, " of ", nrow(wk_cmp), " weeks"),
       subtitle = paste0("Left, 18 Sep. The zone caught ", round(100 * ex_catch), "% of newly burning cells on ",
                         round(100 * ex_land), "% of the land"),
       x = "Week starting", y = "Newly burning cells caught") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 9)))
print(map_ex, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1:3))
print(chart,  vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 4:9))




On the same amount of land, recent fires found more new fires than the hotspot map. The watch zone caught 76 percent of newly burning cells on 15 percent of the land. Hotspot zones caught 64, 58 and 50 percent at 1.5, 3 and 6 km.
The gap to the best hotspot zone is 12 points (95 percent interval 3.6 to 16.3). The watch zone did better on 23 days and worse on 6 (sign test p = 0.0023), and for separate new fires it caught 29 percent against 22. It did slightly worse in the weeks of 3 August and 24 August. Its settings came from this season, so it needs testing on another year.

    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +

}

ggarrange(eda_hist("RADIO", "Radio count"),
          eda_hist("RADIO_PR", "Radio per 1,000 households"),
          eda_box("RADIO"), eda_box("RADIO_PR"),
          ncol = 2, nrow = 2, heights = c(2, 1))




The radio count is strongly right skewed. Its three outliers, Taunggyi, Lashio and Nyaungshwe, are the three townships with the most households. Taunggyi alone has 30,176 radios. The rate is much closer to symmetric, with 1 high outlier left. The top rate is in Ywangan, a small township, and not Taunggyi.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
4.2 Distribution of All Six Rates
The book builds six histograms and joins them with ggarrange(). I use pivot_longer() and facet_wrap() instead, which gives the same six panels from one call.

The PlotThe Code














ict_derived %>%
  select(ends_with("_PR")) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "rate") %>%
  mutate(variable = factor(variable,
                           levels = c("RADIO_PR", "TV_PR", "LLPHONE_PR",
                                      "MPHONE_PR", "COMPUTER_PR", "INTERNET_PR"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rate)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#56B4E9", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, ncol = 3, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Per 1,000 households", y = "Townships",
       title = "TV is the most common item, computers and landlines the rarest") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"))




TV and mobile phone are roughly symmetric. Landline, computer and internet are all right skewed, with most townships near zero and a few far ahead.

4.3 Joining the Two Data Sets
Before joining I check that the township names in the shapefile and the csv agree for every code.

name_check <- shan_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(TS_PCODE, TS) %>%
  inner_join(select(ict_derived, TS_PCODE, TS), by = "TS_PCODE")

c(matched = nrow(name_check),
  same_name = sum(name_check$TS.x == name_check$TS.y))

  matched same_name 
       55        55 


left_join() of dplyr then attaches the rates to the boundaries by TS_PCODE.

shan_sf <- left_join(shan_sf,
                     select(ict_derived, -DT_PCODE, -DT, -TS),
                     by = "TS_PCODE")







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book joins the full table, so the district and township columns appear twice. R renames them TS.x and TS.y, and the rest of the chapter has to use TS.x. All 55 codes match and the names agree in every case, so I drop the duplicate columns from the csv before joining. The township column stays TS. The book also saves and reloads the joined data as an rds file. I skip that because freeze: true already stops the page from re-running.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
4.4 Choropleth Maps
tm_shape() and tm_polygons() of tmap map the number of households, the radio count and the radio rate. Each uses Jenks natural breaks with five classes, as in the book. tmap_arrange() puts them side by side.

Households and radio countHouseholds and radio rateThe Code

























jenks_map <- function(var, legend_title, title) {
  tm_shape(shan_sf) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "jenks", n = 5,
                                                values = "brewer.blues"),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legend_title,
                                        position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
                col = "grey60") +
    tm_title(title, size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")
}

tmap_arrange(jenks_map("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "Households", "Total households"),
             jenks_map("RADIO", "Radios", "Radio count"),
             ncol = 2)

tmap_arrange(jenks_map("TT_HOUSEHOLDS", "Households", "Total households"),
             jenks_map("RADIO_PR", "Per 1,000", "Radio per 1,000 households"),
             ncol = 2)




The household map and the radio count map look almost the same. Both are dark around Taunggyi and Lashio. The rate map is different. Its highest classes run down the west side of the state, while much of the north east is pale. This confirms the rates and not the counts should go into the clustering.






CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book uses tmap v3 code such as tm_fill(style = "jenks"), tm_borders(alpha = 0.5) and qtm(). These give deprecation messages in tmap 4.4, so I rewrote every map in v4 syntax with fill.scale, fill.legend and tm_title(). All legends sit outside the map.

geom_histogram() draws the radio rate three ways, raw, min-max and z-score.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.4 Computing the Proximity Matrix
dist() computes the Euclidean distance between every pair of townships across the five rates.

proxmat <- dist(shan_ict, method = "euclidean")







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book shows both scaling methods and then builds the distance matrix from the raw rates in shan_ict. I do the same in the main part so my results can be checked against the book. But it has a cost. A rate with a wide range adds more to the distance. In the section Raw Rates Against Z-scores I measure how much and rerun the clustering on z-scores.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.5 Selecting the Clustering Algorithm
agnes() of cluster reports an agglomerative coefficient for each linkage method. Values closer to 1 mean a stronger cluster structure. map_dbl() of purrr runs it for four methods.

m <- c("average", "single", "complete", "ward")
names(m) <- c("average", "single", "complete", "ward")

ac <- function(x) {
  agnes(shan_ict, method = x)$ac
}

map_dbl(m, ac)

  average    single  complete      ward 
0.8131144 0.6628705 0.8950702 0.9427730 


Ward’s method gives the highest coefficient, 0.943, so I use it from here on.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.6 Computing the Hierarchical Clustering
hclust() of base R builds the tree with Ward’s method.

hclust_ward <- hclust(proxmat, method = "ward.D2")







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book uses method = "ward.D". R has two Ward options. ward.D2 squares the distances before merging, which is Ward’s original criterion. ward.D does not. The agnes() check above and the hcut() used for the gap statistic below both use the squared version. So ward.D2 keeps the whole section on one method. The two trees do give different results. Cut at six clusters, they only agree with an adjusted Rand index of 0.77, where 1 means identical. So my clusters will not match the book’s.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.7 Determining the Number of Clusters
clusGap() of cluster computes the gap statistic for 1 to 10 clusters. It compares how tight the clusters are with how tight they would be in random data. hcut() of factoextra does the clustering inside it.

set.seed(12345)
gap_stat <- clusGap(shan_ict,
                    FUN = hcut,
                    nstart = 25,
                    K.max = 10,
                    B = 50)
print(gap_stat, method = "firstmax")

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.8 Interpreting the Dendrogram
plot() draws the tree and rect.hclust() boxes the six clusters.

The PlotThe Code














okabe6 <- c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#CC79A7", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#F0E442")

plot(hclust_ward, cex = 0.6, xlab = "", sub = "",
     main = "Ward's tree of Shan townships, cut into six clusters",
     cex.main = 1.5, las = 1)
rect.hclust(hclust_ward, k = 6, border = okabe6)










CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book draws the boxes with border = 2:5. That is four base R colours for six boxes, so two are reused, and one of them is green. I use six Okabe-Ito colours without green, which I set once as okabe6 and reuse for every cluster map below.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.9 Visually-driven Hierarchical Clustering
heatmaply() of heatmaply draws an interactive heatmap with a dendrogram of the rows. It needs a matrix, so data.matrix() converts the data frame first.

shan_ict_mat <- data.matrix(shan_ict)


The PlotThe Code











heatmaply(normalize(shan_ict_mat),
          Colv = NA,
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D2",
          seriate = "OLO",
          colors = Blues,
          k_row = 6,
          margins = c(NA, 200, 60, NA),
          fontsize_row = 4,
          fontsize_col = 5,
          main = "Geographic Segmentation of Shan State by ICT indicators",
          xlab = "ICT Indicators",
          ylab = "Townships of Shan State")










NoteLearning diary



The six row groups in the heatmap are not the same six clusters as the dendrogram above. heatmaply() clusters the data it is given, and here that is normalize(shan_ict_mat), the min-max version. The dendrogram used the raw rates. I first assumed the heatmap was just a picture of my clusters, but it is a second clustering. It is useful for seeing which rates are high or low in each group of rows. The cluster labels should come from cutree().

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
6.10 Mapping the Clusters
cutree() cuts the tree into six groups. I add them to shan_sf as a factor column.

groups <- as.factor(cutree(hclust_ward, k = 6))
shan_sf_cluster <- shan_sf %>%
  mutate(CLUSTER = groups)
table(shan_sf_cluster$CLUSTER)


 1  2  3  4  5  6 
16  8 13  6  7  5 



The PlotThe Code














cluster_map <- function(data, var, title, title_size = 1.5) {
  tm_shape(data) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = okabe6),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Cluster",
                                        position = tm_pos_out("right", "center")),
                col = "grey40") +
    tm_title(title, size = title_size, fontface = "bold")
}

cluster_map(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER",
            "Hierarchical clusters are scattered across the state")




The clusters are fragmented. Most of them appear in several separate places on the map. This is expected, because hierarchical clustering only looks at the ICT rates and not at location. Two townships far apart can end up in the same cluster if their rates are similar. For a segmentation that can be used to plan by region, this is a problem. The next two methods add location.

7.3 Computing the Minimum Spanning Tree
mstree() of spdep finds the minimum spanning tree. This is the set of links that connects all townships with the lowest total cost and no loops.

set.seed(1234)
shan.mst <- mstree(shan.w)
dim(shan.mst)

[1] 54  3

head(shan.mst)

[1,]   28   12  78.78999
[2,]   12   49  59.69478
[3,]   28   13  92.79567
[4,]   13   52 110.55197
[5,]   49   35 124.74445
[6,]   35   37  91.65458


The tree has 54 links for 55 townships, one fewer than the number of townships, as a tree should. Each row gives the two townships and the cost of the link.






NoteLearning diary



mstree() starts from a random township when ini is not given, so I added set.seed(). I tried a few seeds. The start point changed the order of the rows but not the cluster sizes SKATER produced, because the tree itself is the same.



The PlotThe Code














plot(st_geometry(shan_sf), border = "grey60",
     main = "Minimum spanning tree of Shan townships", cex.main = 1.5)

         cex.lab = 0.7, cex.circles = 0.005, add = TRUE)




Compared with the neighbour map, most links are gone. Each township now connects to the rest of the state by only one path.

7.5 Mapping the SKATER Clusters

The PlotThe Code














shan_sf_spatialcluster <- shan_sf_cluster %>%
  mutate(SP_CLUSTER = as.factor(ccs6))

cluster_map(shan_sf_spatialcluster, "SP_CLUSTER",

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
8.1 Ward-like Hierarchical Clustering with ClustGeo
hclustgeo() with only D0 gives the non-spatial version.

The PlotThe Code














nongeo_cluster <- hclustgeo(proxmat)
plot(nongeo_cluster, cex = 0.5, xlab = "", sub = "",
     main = "ClustGeo tree with alpha = 0", cex.main = 1.5, las = 1)
rect.hclust(nongeo_cluster, k = 6, border = okabe6)





ngeo_groups <- as.factor(cutree(nongeo_cluster, k = 6))
shan_sf_ngeo_cluster <- shan_sf %>%
  mutate(CLUSTER = ngeo_groups)

adjustedRandIndex(ngeo_groups, groups)

[1] 1








ImportantCheck that caught something



The book maps these clusters as a new result. I expected them to match my hclust() clusters, since ClustGeo with alpha = 0 is plain Ward clustering. The adjusted Rand index of 1 shows they are the same six groups. ClustGeo squares the distances, like ward.D2. This is also why the book’s two maps differ. The book’s hclust() used ward.D, which does not square them. So I skip the duplicate map.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
8.2 Spatially Constrained Hierarchical Clustering
st_distance() of sf computes the distance between every pair of townships. as.dist() turns it into the D1 matrix.

dist <- st_distance(shan_sf, shan_sf)
distmat <- as.dist(dist)







NoteLearning diary



st_distance() on polygons measures the gap between their boundaries, not their centres. So any two townships that touch have a distance of 0. In this matrix 132 pairs are at 0, the same as the 132 pairs of Queen neighbours. ClustGeo treats them all as equally close, whether they share a long border or one corner.


choicealpha() of ClustGeo tries alpha from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.1. For each alpha it reports two scores. Q0 is the share of ICT variation explained by the six clusters, and Q1 is the share of spatial variation explained. Raising alpha gains Q1 and loses Q0.

cr <- choicealpha(proxmat, distmat,
                  range.alpha = seq(0, 1, 0.1),
                  K = 6, graph = FALSE)


The PlotThe Code














alpha_df <- tibble(alpha = cr$range.alpha,
                   `Q0, ICT` = cr$Q[, 1],
                   `Q1, location` = cr$Q[, 2]) %>%
  pivot_longer(-alpha, names_to = "score", values_to = "value")

ggplot(alpha_df, aes(x = alpha, y = value, colour = score)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.2, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "alpha", y = "Share of variation explained", colour = NULL,
       title = "Most of the spatial gain comes by alpha = 0.2",
       subtitle = "Dashed line, the alpha used below") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "top")




At alpha 0, the clusters explain 76 percent of the ICT variation but only 13 percent of the spatial variation. At alpha 0.2, Q1 jumps to 63 percent while Q0 only falls to 65 percent. After 0.2, each step gives up roughly as much Q0 as it gains in Q1. So 0.2 is a fair compromise, and it is the value the book uses.






CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book sets graph = TRUE and uses ClustGeo’s own plot. I set it to FALSE and draw Q0 and Q1 with ggplot, so the chart has a title, labelled axes and the chosen alpha marked.


hclustgeo() with both matrices and alpha = 0.2 gives the spatially constrained tree.

clustG <- hclustgeo(proxmat, distmat, alpha = 0.2)
groups_geo <- as.factor(cutree(clustG, k = 6))
shan_sf_Gcluster <- shan_sf %>%
  mutate(CLUSTER = groups_geo)
table(shan_sf_Gcluster$CLUSTER)


 1  2  3  4  5  6 
10  9  7  9 12  8 



The PlotThe Code














tmap_arrange(cluster_map(shan_sf_ngeo_cluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "ClustGeo, alpha = 0", title_size = 1.3),
             cluster_map(shan_sf_Gcluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "ClustGeo, alpha = 0.2", title_size = 1.3),
             ncol = 2)




With alpha 0.2 the clusters are much more compact than at alpha 0, and the sizes are more even, from 7 to 12 townships. But some clusters still have a few townships away from the main block. ClustGeo only pushes nearby townships together. It does not forbid a cluster from being split.

text:
10.1 Raw Rates Against Z-scores
The book clusters on raw rates. To see how much each rate counts, I compare their variances. The squared Euclidean distance is a sum over the five rates, so each rate’s share of the total variance is roughly its share of the distance.

tibble(variable = names(shan_ict),
       sd = sapply(shan_ict, sd),
       share_of_variance = sapply(shan_ict, var) / sum(sapply(shan_ict, var))) %>%
  arrange(desc(share_of_variance)) %>%
  kable(digits = c(0, 1, 3))

MPHONE_PR and TV_PR together make up 81 percent of the variance. COMPUTER_PR makes up less than 1 percent. So the raw clustering mostly ignores computer ownership, even though it is one of the five chosen measures.
I rerun the same Ward clustering on the z-scores, where every rate counts equally.

hclust_z <- hclust(dist(shan_ict.z), method = "ward.D2")
groups_z <- as.factor(cutree(hclust_z, k = 6))
shan_sf_zcluster <- shan_sf %>% mutate(CLUSTER = groups_z)

adjustedRandIndex(groups, groups_z)

[1] 0.317144



The PlotThe Code














tmap_arrange(cluster_map(shan_sf_cluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "Raw rates", title_size = 1.3),
             cluster_map(shan_sf_zcluster, "CLUSTER",
                         "Z-scores", title_size = 1.3),
             ncol = 2)










TipAlternative explored



The two results agree with an adjusted Rand index of only 0.32. Scaling changed the clusters a lot, not just at the edges. With z-scores, landline and computer rates count as much as TV and mobile. The six most connected townships under the raw rates were Muse, Tachileik, Laukkaing, Mongla, Namhkan and Taunggyi. Under z-scores that top group shrinks to Muse, Tachileik, Taunggyi, the three townships with the highest computer rates. Laukkaing and Namhkan move to a group with the most landlines, and Mongla joins a middle group.
Neither version is wrong. They answer different questions. The raw version groups townships mostly by TV and mobile phone use. The z-score version weighs all five measures equally. Since the book chose five measures on purpose, I think the z-score version fits the question better.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
10.2 How Many Clusters
The gap statistic picked one cluster. I check six against two other common measures for the same Ward tree. The average silhouette width shows how well each township fits its own cluster compared with the next closest, and higher is better. The elbow method shows how much within-cluster variation is left as clusters are added.

k_check <- tibble(k = 2:10) %>%
  mutate(silhouette = map_dbl(k, ~ mean(silhouette(cutree(hclust_ward, .x),
                                                   proxmat)[, 3])),
         unexplained = map_dbl(k, ~ 1 - r_squared(cutree(hclust_ward, .x))))


The PlotThe Code














k_plot <- function(y, ylab, title) {
  ggplot(k_check, aes(x = k, y = .data[[y]])) +
    geom_line(colour = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(aes(colour = k == 6), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2:10) +
    labs(x = "Number of clusters", y = ylab, title = title) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
}

ggarrange(k_plot("silhouette", "Average silhouette width",
                 "Silhouette is best at two clusters"),
          k_plot("unexplained", "Share of variation left",
                 "No clear elbow"),
          ncol = 2)










TipAlternative explored



None of the three measures points to six. The silhouette is highest at two clusters, 0.347. At six it is 0.253, the lowest of all the values I tried. The elbow curve falls smoothly with no clear bend. Six clusters still leave 24 percent of the variation unexplained.
So six is a choice for usefulness, not something the data shows. Two clusters would only split the more connected townships from the less connected ones. That is too coarse for planning, so six is reasonable. But a silhouette around 0.25 means the clusters overlap a lot, and townships near the edges could easily go either way.

title: Hands-on Exercise 6
text:
10.3 What the Spatial Constraint Costs
I put the three main results in one table. It shows how much ICT variation each one explains, how many separate pieces it makes on the map, and how close it is to the plain hclust() result.

solutions <- list(`Hierarchical (ward.D2)` = groups,
                  `SKATER` = ccs6,
                  `ClustGeo, alpha = 0.2` = groups_geo)

cost_table <- tibble(method = names(solutions),
       ict_explained = map_dbl(solutions, r_squared),
       map_pieces = map_dbl(solutions, count_pieces),
       cluster_sizes = map_chr(solutions,
                               ~ paste(sort(table(.x), decreasing = TRUE),
                                       collapse = ", ")),
       ari_vs_hierarchical = map_dbl(solutions,
                                     ~ adjustedRandIndex(.x, groups)))
kable(cost_table, digits = 2)

TipAlternative explored



The table shows the trade-off in numbers. Hierarchical clustering explains the most ICT variation, 76 percent, but its six clusters break into 28 separate pieces on the map. SKATER gives exactly 6 pieces, one per cluster, but explains only 50 percent, and it has single-township clusters. ClustGeo sits in between, with 65 percent explained and 18 pieces.
I expected ClustGeo at alpha 0.2 to look much like SKATER, because the map was so much tidier than at alpha 0. But 18 pieces is still a lot of fragments. Most of them come from clusters 3 and 4, the least and the most connected townships. Extreme townships have no similar neighbours, so ClustGeo leaves them where their rates fit. Both spatial methods are also far from the hierarchical result, with adjusted Rand indexes of 0.18 and 0.26. So the choice of method changes the answer more than any setting within a method.
For planning by region I would use SKATER, because the clusters have to be single areas. I would merge its tiny clusters into their neighbours. ClustGeo is better when a few separate townships are acceptable and the clusters need to stay similar inside.

5.1 Distribution of the Selling Price
mutate() adds a log of the selling price, and geom_histogram() of ggplot2 draws both versions.

condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(LOG_SELLING_PRICE = log(SELLING_PRICE))


The PlotThe Code














price_hist <- function(var, title, xlab) {
  ggplot(condo_resale.sf, aes(x = .data[[var]])) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#56B4E9", colour = "white") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = "Sales", title = title) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"))
}

ggarrange(price_hist("SELLING_PRICE", "Selling price is strongly right skewed",
                     "Selling price (S$)"),
          price_hist("LOG_SELLING_PRICE", "The log of price is much closer to symmetric",
                     "log(selling price)"),

The middle half of the units sold for between S$1.1 million and S$1.95 million, but a few sold for over S$10 million, up to S$18 million. These stretch the right tail. The log brings the skewness down from 5.03 to 1.09. The book creates the log variable but never uses it in a model. I come back to it in Log Price Instead of Price.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9
text:
5.2 Distribution of the Independent Variables
The book builds twelve histograms and joins them with ggarrange(). pivot_longer() and facet_wrap() give the same panels from one call.

The PlotThe Code














condo_resale.sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(AREA_SQM, AGE, PROX_CBD, PROX_CHILDCARE, PROX_ELDERLYCARE,
         PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA, PROX_HAWKER_MARKET, PROX_KINDERGARTEN,
         PROX_MRT, PROX_PARK, PROX_PRIMARY_SCH, PROX_TOP_PRIMARY_SCH) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(variable = fct_inorder(variable)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#56B4E9", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, ncol = 4, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Sales",
       title = "Floor area and most distances are right skewed") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"))




The distances are in kilometres. Most are right skewed, with many condos close to each facility and a few far away. PROX_CBD is the exception, with a wide spread from the city centre out to the edges of the island.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9
text:
5.3 Statistical Point Map
tm_shape() and tm_dots() of tmap map the selling price of each sale over the subzone boundaries, using quantile classes.

The PlotThe Code














tmap_mode("plot")
tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey75") +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "SELLING_PRICE",
          size = 0.25,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                          values = "brewer.blues",
                                          values.range = c(0.25, 1)),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Selling price (S$)",

The darkest points, the top fifth of prices, are packed into the central area near the CBD. The cheaper sales are spread across the east, north and west. So price already looks spatially clustered before any model is fitted.






CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book draws this map and the later point maps in tmap_mode("view"), as interactive web maps. I use static plot mode with the legend outside the map. A static map shows in the rendered page without loading web map tiles, and it keeps the same look as my other exercises. The book’s view-mode code for the local R² and coefficient maps also uses tmap v3 arguments such as col and border.col, which I rewrote in v4 syntax.

NoteLearning diary



Some signs look odd at first. PROX_CHILDCARE, PROX_MRT and PROX_SHOPPING_MALL are negative, which makes sense, since being further from these lowers the price. But PROX_PARK, PROX_ELDERLYCARE and PROX_BUS_STOP are positive, so being further from a park or a bus stop goes with a higher price. I think these pick up other things. Expensive condos in the central area are often not right next to a big park, and bus stops are densest in the HDB towns. A global model cannot separate these, which is one reason to try GWR.

The PlotThe Code














plot(mlr.vif, colors = c("#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(title = "Every VIF is well below 5") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"))




The highest VIF is 3.26, for PROX_CHILDCARE. All are far below the usual cut-off of 10, so multicollinearity is not a problem.


6.5.2 Linearity
check_model() with check = "linearity" plots the residuals against the fitted values.

The PlotThe Code














check_model(condo.mlr1, check = "linearity",
            colors = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#CC79A7"))




Up to fitted prices of about S$5 million, where most sales are, the residuals scatter around zero. Above that the reference line curves up steeply, because the most expensive condos sold for far more than the model predicts. So the straight-line form works for most of the market but not for the top end. The spread also widens for the higher fitted prices, which is a sign of unequal variance.


6.5.3 Normality
check_normality() runs a Shapiro-Wilk test on the standardised residuals.

check_normality(condo.mlr1)

Warning: Non-normality of residuals detected (p < .001).



The PlotThe Code














qq_plot <- plot(check_normality(condo.mlr1), type = "qq")
line_layers <- sapply(qq_plot$layers, function(l)
  inherits(l$geom, c("GeomPath", "GeomAbline", "GeomHline", "GeomSegment")))
for (i in which(line_layers)) qq_plot$layers[[i]]$aes_params$colour <- "#D55E00"

qq_plot +
  labs(title = "The residuals leave the line at both ends") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"))










ImportantCheck that caught something



The book says the Q-Q plot shows most points along the line and that the residuals resemble a normal distribution. The test disagrees strongly. The Shapiro-Wilk W is 0.686, and the skewness of the residuals is 5.14. A normal distribution has W close to 1 and skewness 0. The points do follow the line in the middle, but the top end bends far away because of the very expensive sales. This matters because the p-values in the table assume normal errors. The book’s note that formal tests reject too easily in large samples is true, but here the plot shows the same problem. I test a log-price model in Log Price Instead of Price.


The book also draws the same check through check_model(). It shows the same pattern as the Q-Q plot above, so I leave it out.


6.5.4 Spatial Autocorrelation in the Residuals
The model uses located data, so the residuals may be spatially autocorrelated. If nearby condos have similar residuals, the model is missing something about location. cbind() adds the residuals to the sf data frame.

condo_resale.sf <- cbind(condo_resale.sf,
                         condo.mlr1$residuals) %>%
  rename(MLR_RES = condo.mlr1.residuals)


The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey75") +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "MLR_RES",
          size = 0.25,
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 10,
                                          style = "quantile",
                                          values = "-brewer.rd_bu",
                                          midpoint = NA),
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "OLS residual (S$)",
                                  position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_title("OLS residuals of the same sign sit together",
           size = 1.5, fontface = "bold")




Red points are under-predicted, where the model guesses too low, and blue points are over-predicted. Both colours come in groups rather than being mixed at random.
To test this, st_dist_band() of sfdep links every pair of condos within 1,500 m, and st_weights() row-standardises the links.

condo_resale.sf <- condo_resale.sf %>%
  mutate(nb = st_dist_band(st_geometry(geometry),
                           upper = 1500),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)

Each condo has between 1 and 125 neighbours within 1,500 m, with a median of 42. global_moran_perm() then runs the permutation test, as in the book.

set.seed(1234)
global_moran_perm(condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES,
                  nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
                  wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
                  alternative = "two.sided",
                  nsim = 499)


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  x 
weights: listw  
number of simulations + 1: 500 

statistic = 0.14389, observed rank = 500, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


Moran’s I is 0.144, above 0, so the residuals are clustered. Nearby condos tend to be over- or under-predicted together.






ImportantCheck that caught something



The report gives a p-value below 2.2e-16. With 499 shuffles, that is impossible. The real map is compared with 499 shuffled maps, so the smallest possible one-sided p-value is 1/500 = 0.002. For the two-sided test, spdep’s formula returns exactly 0 when the real map beats every shuffle, which R then prints as below 2.2e-16. alternative = "greater" gives the honest value.

set.seed(1234)
mlr_moran <- global_moran_perm(condo_resale.sf$MLR_RES,
                               nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
                               wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
                               alternative = "greater",
                               nsim = 499)
mlr_moran


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  x 
weights: listw  
number of simulations + 1: 500 

statistic = 0.14389, observed rank = 500, p-value = 0.002
alternative hypothesis: greater


The p-value is 0.002, the smallest the test can give. The conclusion is the same, but the true strength of the evidence is “beats all 499 shuffles”, not “p below 2.2e-16”.

bw.gwr() of GWmodel searches for the bandwidth with the lowest cross-validation (CV) score. adaptive = FALSE asks for a fixed distance.

    FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "gaussian",
  adaptive = FALSE,
  longlat = FALSE)

title: Hands-on Exercise 9
text:
7.3 Comparing the Three Models
The two GWR reports each include the global OLS model at the top. I put the main numbers side by side. AICc rewards fit but penalises extra parameters, and lower is better.

aicc_lm <- function(m) {
  k <- length(coef(m)) + 1
  n <- nobs(m)
  AIC(m) + 2 * k * (k + 1) / (n - k - 1)
}

model_compare <- tibble(
  model = c("OLS", "GWR, fixed bandwidth", "GWR, adaptive bandwidth"),
  bandwidth = c("none",
                paste0(round(bw.fixed), " m"),
                paste0(bw.adaptive, " neighbours")),
  r2 = c(summary(condo.mlr1)$r.squared,
         gwr.fixed$GW.diagnostic$gw.R2,
         gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$gw.R2),
  adj_r2 = c(summary(condo.mlr1)$adj.r.squared,
             gwr.fixed$GW.diagnostic$gwR2.adj,
             gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$gwR2.adj),
  AICc = c(aicc_lm(condo.mlr1),
           gwr.fixed$GW.diagnostic$AICc,
           gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$AICc),
  effective_parameters = c(length(coef(condo.mlr1)),
                           gwr.fixed$GW.diagnostic$enp,
                           gwr.adaptive$GW.diagnostic$enp))
kable(model_compare, digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 1, 1))

NoteLearning diary



The last column was new to me. OLS uses 15 parameters. The adaptive GWR behaves like a model with about 350 parameters, because every condo has its own set of 15 coefficients, smoothed by the kernel. That is a lot for 1,436 sales. AICc already penalises it, and GWR still wins, but it means some of the local coefficients are fitted from very little data. I look at how reliable they are in Which Local Effects Can Be Trusted.

7.4 Converting the SDF into an sf Data Frame

CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book’s list of output fields includes a condition number for local collinearity, with a warning that values above 30 are unreliable. gwr.basic() does not return that field, as the glimpse() above shows. GWmodel computes local condition numbers in a separate function, gwr.collin.diagno(). 7.5 Visualising Local R²

The PlotThe Code














tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey75") +
tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +
  tm_dots(fill = "Local_R2",

                                          values = "brewer.purples",

Local R² ranges from 0.67 to 0.99, with a median of 0.91. Even the weakest local model explains about two thirds of the variation. The fit is weakest near the city centre. For condos within 3 km of the CBD the median local R² is 0.87, against 0.96 for those more than 10 km away. Central prices probably depend more on things the 14 variables do not record, such as the view, the floor level or the prestige of the development.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9
text:
7.6 Visualising the Coefficient Estimates
The book maps the standard error and the t-value of the AREA_SQM coefficient side by side. tmap_arrange() puts the two maps next to each other.

The PlotThe Code














coef_map <- function(var, title, legend_title, palette) {
  tm_shape(mpsz_svy21) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey75") +
  tm_shape(condo_resale.sf.adaptive) +
    tm_dots(fill = var,
            size = 0.2,
            fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile",
                                            values = palette,
                                            values.range = c(0.25, 1)),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legend_title,
                                    position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
    tm_title(title, size = 1.3, fontface = "bold")
}

tmap_arrange(coef_map("AREA_SQM_SE", "Standard error of AREA_SQM",
                      "Std. error", "brewer.oranges"),
             coef_map("AREA_SQM_TV", "t-value of AREA_SQM",
                      "t-value", "brewer.blues"),
             ncol = 2)




The t-value is above 1.96 at 1376 of the 1,436 condos, so floor area matters almost everywhere. The t-values are highest in the central area and much lower in the north, east and west, where the remaining 60 condos that are not significant all sit, between 10 and 17 km from the CBD. The standard error map is almost the reverse. It is largest in the outer areas.
The reason shows up in the coefficient itself. The local value of an extra square metre ranges from S$3,319 to S$23,064, against a single S$12,778 in the OLS model. Within 3 km of the CBD the median is S$14,092 per square metre, and beyond 10 km it is S$5,499. A square metre costs much more in the centre, so the effect there is large relative to its error. In the suburbs the effect is smaller, and the same amount of noise makes it less certain. This is the kind of local difference a single OLS coefficient hides.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9
text:
8.1 Log Price Instead of Price
The book makes LOG_SELLING_PRICE in the EDA but then models the raw price. I refit the revised OLS model with the log of price and compare the two on the problems found in the diagnostics.

condo.mlr1.log <- lm(
  formula = log(SELLING_PRICE) ~ AREA_SQM + AGE +
    PROX_CBD + PROX_CHILDCARE + PROX_MRT +
    PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_URA_GROWTH_AREA +
    PROX_PARK + PROX_PRIMARY_SCH +
    PROX_SHOPPING_MALL + PROX_BUS_STOP +
    NO_Of_UNITS + FAMILY_FRIENDLY + FREEHOLD,
  data = condo_resale.sf)

set.seed(1234)
log_moran <- global_moran_perm(residuals(condo.mlr1.log),
                               nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
                               wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
                               alternative = "greater",
                               nsim = 499)

skew <- function(x) mean(scale(x)^3)

log_compare <- tibble(
  check = c("Adjusted R²", "Shapiro-Wilk W of residuals",
            "Skewness of residuals", "Breusch-Pagan statistic",
            "Moran's I of residuals", "Variables significant at 0.05"),
  price = c(summary(condo.mlr1)$adj.r.squared,
            shapiro.test(residuals(condo.mlr1))$statistic,
            skew(residuals(condo.mlr1)),
            bptest(condo.mlr1)$statistic,
            mlr_moran$statistic,
            sum(coef(summary(condo.mlr1))[-1, 4] < 0.05)),
  log_price = c(summary(condo.mlr1.log)$adj.r.squared,
                shapiro.test(residuals(condo.mlr1.log))$statistic,
                skew(residuals(condo.mlr1.log)),
                bptest(condo.mlr1.log)$statistic,
                log_moran$statistic,
                sum(coef(summary(condo.mlr1.log))[-1, 4] < 0.05)))
log_compare %>%
  mutate(across(c(price, log_price),
                ~ if_else(check == "Variables significant at 0.05",
                          as.character(round(.x)), sprintf("%.3f", .x)))) %>%
  kable(align = "lrr")

The log model fixes most of the normality problem. The residual skewness drops from 5.14 to -0.19 and W rises from 0.686 to 0.972. The fit also improves, with the adjusted R² going from 0.647 to 0.786. This makes sense for prices. Features tend to add a percentage to the price rather than a fixed amount, so an extra square metre is worth more in an expensive area. The log model reads that way. For example, freehold tenure adds about 16 percent to the price.
Two problems remain. The Breusch-Pagan test still finds unequal variance, and the residuals are even more clustered, with Moran’s I at 0.200 against 0.144 for the price model. The log also changes which variables matter. Only 10 of the 14 stay significant. PROX_CHILDCARE, PROX_PRIMARY_SCH, NO_Of_UNITS, and FAMILY_FRIENDLY drop out, so their effect in the price model came mostly from the expensive end. So the log model is better behaved, but it still needs a spatial model. The book’s GWR on raw price is a fair choice for teaching, but a log-price GWR would be the next thing I would try.

section: 8.2 Does GWR Remove the Spatial Autocorrelation?
text:
8.2 Does GWR Remove the Spatial Autocorrelation?
The OLS residuals were clustered, which was the reason to try GWR. I run the same Moran’s I test on the residuals of both GWR models, with the same 1,500 m weights.

moran_res <- function(res) {
  set.seed(1234)
  global_moran_perm(res,
                    nb = condo_resale.sf$nb,
                    wt = condo_resale.sf$wt,
                    alternative = "greater",
                    nsim = 499)
}

gwr_fixed_moran <- moran_res(gwr.fixed$SDF$residual)
gwr_adaptive_moran <- moran_res(gwr.adaptive$SDF$residual)

tibble(model = c("OLS", "GWR, fixed bandwidth", "GWR, adaptive bandwidth"),
       morans_I = c(mlr_moran$statistic,
                    gwr_fixed_moran$statistic,
                    gwr_adaptive_moran$statistic),
       p_value = c(mlr_moran$p.value,
                   gwr_fixed_moran$p.value,
                   gwr_adaptive_moran$p.value)) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)

tmap_arrange(res_map(condo_resale.sf, "MLR_RES", "OLS residuals"),

             ncol = 2)










TipAlternative explored



GWR removes the clustering. Moran’s I falls from 0.144 for OLS to -0.016 for the adaptive GWR, with a p-value of 0.988. The fixed model gives -0.020. Both are slightly below zero and nowhere near significant. On the maps I used the same fixed classes for both models so they can be compared. The GWR map has far more grey points within S$100,000 of the actual price, and the large errors no longer come in groups.
The book shows that GWR fits better, but it does not check whether GWR fixed the problem that motivated it. Here it did. The caution is that a model with about 350 effective parameters can absorb almost any spatial pattern, so this result shows the residuals are clean, not that every local coefficient is meaningful. The next section looks at that.

5.2 Row-standardised Weights Matrix
nb2listw() of spdep turns the neighbour list into weights. style = "W" divides each county’s weights by its number of neighbours. So the lag of a county is the simple average of its neighbours.

rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
rswm_q

zero.policy = TRUE lets spdep accept a county with no neighbours instead of stopping with an error. Hunan has no such county, so it changes nothing here. The book always sets it, and it matters for data with islands.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
6.1 Moran’s I Test
moran.test() of spdep computes Moran’s I. It tests it against the null hypothesis that GDPPC is spread across the counties at random. The default alternative is "greater", so the test only looks for positive autocorrelation.

moran_gdppc <- moran.test(hunan$GDPPC,
                          listw = rswm_q,
                          zero.policy = TRUE,
                          na.action = na.omit)
moran_gdppc


    Moran I test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC  
weights: rswm_q    

Moran I statistic standard deviate = 4.7351, p-value = 1.095e-06
alternative hypothesis: greater
sample estimates:
Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
      0.300749970      -0.011494253       0.004348351 


Moran’s I is 0.301 against an expected value of -0.0115 under randomness. The p-value is 1.1e-06, far below 0.05, so I reject the null hypothesis. GDPPC in Hunan is positively autocorrelated. Rich counties tend to sit next to rich counties and poor ones next to poor ones.






ImportantCheck that caught something



In Exercise 4 I predicted this number before running any test. The slope of the neighbour average on GDPPC was 0.301. I argued that with row-standardised weights this slope equals Moran’s I. The test gives the same value to three decimals, so I was right. moran.test() adds the p-value.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
6.2 Computing Monte Carlo Moran’s I
moran.mc() of spdep runs a permutation test instead. It shuffles GDPPC across the 88 counties 999 times and computes Moran’s I for each shuffle. Then it counts how often a shuffle beats the real map. set.seed() makes the result the same on every render.

set.seed(1234)
bperm <- moran.mc(hunan$GDPPC,
                  listw = rswm_q,
                  nsim = 999,
                  zero.policy = TRUE,
                  na.action = na.omit)
bperm


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.30075, observed rank = 1000, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater


The observed I ranks 1000 out of 1000, above all 999 shuffles. This gives a p-value of 0.001, the same conclusion as the analytical test. A random arrangement of these values does not produce this clustering.






NoteLearning diary



The p-value of 0.001 is the lowest possible value here. With 999 shuffles plus the real map there are 1,000 values. The real map can at best rank first, so the smallest p-value is 1/1000. Running 9,999 shuffles would lower this floor but not change the conclusion. The analytical test can go much smaller because it uses a normal approximation instead of counting.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
6.3 Visualising Monte Carlo Moran’s I
mean(), var() and summary() describe the 999 simulated values. bperm$res also holds the observed I as its last element. This is why the book slices [1:999].

mean(bperm$res[1:999])

[1] -0.01504572

var(bperm$res[1:999])

[1] 0.004371574

summary(bperm$res[1:999])

    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
-0.18339 -0.06168 -0.02125 -0.01505  0.02611  0.27593 


The book asks me to redraw the histogram with ggplot2 instead of base graphics. geom_histogram() draws the 999 simulated values. The dashed line marks the expected value under randomness, -1/(n - 1), and the orange line marks the observed I.

The PlotThe Code














mc_moran <- tibble(sim = bperm$res[1:999])

ggplot(mc_moran, aes(x = sim)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#56B4E9", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -1 / (nrow(hunan) - 1),
             linetype = 2, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bperm$statistic,
             colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = bperm$statistic, y = Inf,
           label = paste0("Observed I = ", round(bperm$statistic, 3)),
           hjust = 1.05, vjust = 1.5, colour = "#D55E00", size = 4.5) +
  labs(x = "Simulated Moran's I", y = "Frequency",
       title = "Moran's I, 999 shuffles against the real map",
       subtitle = "Dashed line, expected I under randomness, -1/87") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"))




The shuffles centre on -0.015, close to the expected -1/87, with a standard deviation of about 0.066. The highest of the 999 is 0.276. The observed 0.301 is beyond all of them, which matches the rank of 1000. The simulated distribution is slightly skewed to the right, so the normal approximation behind moran.test() is only approximate.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
7.1 Geary’s C Test
geary.test() of spdep computes Geary’s C. It works the opposite way to Moran’s I. The expected value under randomness is 1. Values below 1 mean neighbours are similar, and values above 1 mean they are different.

geary_gdppc <- geary.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = rswm_q)
geary_gdppc


    Geary C test under randomisation

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q   

Geary C statistic standard deviate = 3.6108, p-value = 0.0001526
alternative hypothesis: Expectation greater than statistic
sample estimates:
Geary C statistic       Expectation          Variance 
        0.6907223         1.0000000         0.0073364 


Geary’s C is 0.691, below the expected 1, with a p-value of 0.00015. So Geary’s C also rejects randomness. Like Moran’s I, it shows positive autocorrelation.






NoteLearning diary



The two statistics are built differently, so they can disagree. Moran’s I multiplies each county’s deviation from the mean by its neighbours’ deviations. It is a covariance and responds to the overall trend across the province. Geary’s C squares the difference between each pair of neighbours. It is closer to a local variance and responds more to sharp differences between next-door counties. Here they agree.

text:
7.2 Computing Monte Carlo Geary’s C
geary.mc() of spdep runs the same permutation idea for Geary’s C.

set.seed(1234)
bperm_c <- geary.mc(hunan$GDPPC,
                    listw = rswm_q,
                    nsim = 999)
bperm_c


    Monte-Carlo simulation of Geary C

data:  hunan$GDPPC 
weights: rswm_q  
number of simulations + 1: 1000 

statistic = 0.69072, observed rank = 1, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: greater








CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book stores this result in bperm again, which overwrites the Moran’s I permutations. I call it bperm_c so both stay available for the comparison below.


The observed C ranks 1, lower than every shuffle. For Geary’s C the small end is the extreme end. So a rank of 1 gives the same lowest p-value of 0.001.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
8.1 Compute Moran’s I Correlogram
sp.correlogram() of spdep computes Moran’s I at lags 1 to 6 with row-standardised weights.

MI_corr <- sp.correlogram(wm_q,
                          hunan$GDPPC,
                          order = 6,
                          method = "I",
                          style = "W")


The PlotThe Code














plot_corr(corr_table(MI_corr), "Moran's I",
          "Moran's I correlogram of GDPPC")




print() shows the numbers behind the plot, with a p-value for each lag.

print(MI_corr)

Spatial correlogram for hunan$GDPPC 
method: Moran's I
         estimate expectation   variance standard deviate Pr(I) two sided    
1 (88)  0.3007500  -0.0114943  0.0043484           4.7351       2.189e-06 ***
2 (88)  0.2060084  -0.0114943  0.0020962           4.7505       2.029e-06 ***
3 (88)  0.0668273  -0.0114943  0.0014602           2.0496        0.040400 *  
4 (88)  0.0299470  -0.0114943  0.0011717           1.2107        0.226015    
5 (88) -0.1530471  -0.0114943  0.0012440          -4.0134       5.984e-05 ***
6 (88) -0.1187070  -0.0114943  0.0016791          -2.6164        0.008886 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Similarity fades with distance and then turns negative. Lags 1 to 3 are positive and significant, at 0.30, 0.21 and 0.07. So a county is like its neighbours and its neighbours’ neighbours. Lag 4 looks random. Lags 5 and 6 are negative and significant, so counties five steps apart tend to be unlike each other. This fits one rich core with a poorer area around it. Five steps from the Changsha block reaches the far west and south, the other end of the income scale.
The p-values in print() are two-sided and not corrected. Six tests at 0.05 is a small multiple testing problem. But lags 1, 2 and 5 are so far below any threshold that the conclusion holds.

        estimate expectation  variance standard deviate Pr(I) two sided    
1 (88) 0.6907223   1.0000000 0.0073364          -3.6108       0.0003052 ***
2 (88) 0.7630197   1.0000000 0.0049126          -3.3811       0.0007220 ***
3 (88) 0.9397299   1.0000000 0.0049005          -0.8610       0.3892612

Geary’s C gives the same result in reverse. It is below 1 at lags 1 and 2, near 1 at lags 3 and 4, and above 1 at lag 5. It is less certain at the ends. Lags 3 and 6 are significant for Moran’s I but not for Geary’s C. This fits the learning diary note above. Geary’s C uses squared differences between the counties being compared. So it responds more to how alike those pairs are, and less to the broad north east against south west trend that Moran’s I picks up.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
10.1 Plotting the Moran Scatterplot
st_lag() of sfdep computes the spatial lag, the average GDPPC of each county’s neighbours.

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(lag_GDPPC = st_lag(GDPPC, nb, wt),
         .before = 1)







CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book follows st_lag() with unnest(lag_GDPPC). st_lag() already returns a plain numeric vector with one value per county. There is nothing to unnest, so I leave that step out.


The Moran scatterplot puts each county’s GDPPC on the x axis and its lag on the y axis. Dashed lines split it into four quadrants. The colour is the quadrant sfdep assigned in the mean column. geom_text_repel() of ggrepel names the counties in the two outlier quadrants.

The PlotThe Code














ggplot(lisa, aes(x = GDPPC, y = lag_GDPPC)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(lisa$GDPPC), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(lisa$GDPPC), linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = mean), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(lisa, mean %in% c("High-Low", "Low-High"),
                                GDPPC > 40000 | lag_GDPPC > 40000),
                  aes(label = NAME_3), size = 3.5, seed = 42,
                  box.padding = 0.5, min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("High-High" = "#D55E00", "Low-Low" = "#0072B2",
                                 "Low-High" = "#56B4E9", "High-Low" = "#CC79A7")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "GDPPC (RMB)", y = "Spatial lag of GDPPC (RMB)", colour = "Quadrant",
       title = "Moran scatterplot with LISA quadrants") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"))










CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book’s note says the upper right quadrant holds counties with high GDPPC “surrounded by average-level neighbouring areas”. This does not match what the quadrant means. Upper right is above the mean on both axes. So it is a High-High county, with high GDPPC and neighbours that are also high on average. Counties with average neighbours would sit near the horizontal dashed line, not in a corner.


The book draws the horizontal line at the mean of the lag. I draw both lines at the mean of GDPPC, because that is where the quadrant labels are cut. spdep, which sfdep calls underneath, centres GDPPC at its mean and then lags the centred values. So a county has high neighbours when its lag is above the mean of GDPPC, not the mean of the lag. summarise() counts how many counties’ labels agree with each line.

lisa %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(label_high = str_detect(mean, "-High$")) %>%
  summarise(`Line at mean of GDPPC` = sum((lag_GDPPC > mean(GDPPC)) == label_high),
            `Line at mean of the lag` = sum((lag_GDPPC > mean(lag_GDPPC)) == label_high))

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  `Line at mean of GDPPC` `Line at mean of the lag`
                    <int>                     <int>
1                      88                        88


Both lines agree with all 88 labels. No county’s lag falls in the narrow gap between the mean of GDPPC and the mean of the lag. So here the book’s line and mine give the same quadrants. The difference only matters when a county sits in that gap.
The plot shows where the 0.30 comes from. Most counties are bottom left, poor with poor neighbours. The High-High group around Changsha pulls the line up. Pingjiang is the clearest Low-High county, a poor county whose neighbours average over 55,000 RMB. Zixing and Lengshuijiang are the clearest High-Low counties, rich mining towns among poorer ones. The LISA map shows which of these are significant.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
section: 10.2 Plotting the Moran Scatterplot with Standardised Variable
text:
10.2 Plotting the Moran Scatterplot with Standardised Variable
scale() turns GDPPC into z-scores. The axes are then in standard deviations and the quadrant lines sit at zero. st_lag() then lags the z-scores.

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(z_GDPPC = as.numeric(scale(GDPPC)),
         z_lag_GDPPC = st_lag(z_GDPPC, nb, wt),
         .before = 1)


The PlotThe Code














ggplot(lisa, aes(x = z_GDPPC, y = z_lag_GDPPC)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = mean), size = 2.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("High-High" = "#D55E00", "Low-Low" = "#0072B2",
                                 "Low-High" = "#56B4E9", "High-Low" = "#CC79A7")) +
  labs(x = "Standardised GDPPC", y = "Standardised spatial lag of GDPPC",
       colour = "Quadrant",
       title = "Standardised Moran scatterplot with LISA quadrants") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"))










CautionWhere I differ from the book



The book standardises the lag separately with scale(lag_GDPPC), which divides it by its own standard deviation. This turns the slope of the fitted line into the simple correlation between a county and its neighbours, 0.485. It also puts the horizontal zero at the mean of the lag, which is not where the quadrant labels are cut.
Anselin’s standardised Moran scatterplot lags the z-scores instead. Both axes are divided by the same standard deviation. The slope stays at Moran’s I, and zero on both axes is exactly the quadrant boundary. The fitted slope here is 0.301, the same as moran.test(). I also wrap scale() in as.numeric(), because it returns a one-column matrix rather than a vector.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
10.3 Preparing LISA Map Classes
signif holds the significance level, so I only set it in one place.

signif <- 0.05

mutate() keeps the quadrant from the mean column where p_ii is below signif. Everything else is labelled Insignificant. factor() fixes the order of the classes, which also fixes the order of the colours on the map.

lisa <- lisa %>%
  mutate(LISA_cluster = if_else(p_ii < signif,
                                as.character(mean),
                                "Insignificant"),
         LISA_cluster = factor(LISA_cluster,
                               levels = c("Insignificant", "Low-Low", "Low-High",
                                          "High-Low", "High-High")))

count(st_drop_geometry(lisa), LISA_cluster)

  LISA_cluster      n
  <fct>         <int>
1 Insignificant    75
2 Low-Low           2
3 Low-High          2

Thirteen counties are significant at 0.05, which answers the book’s question about the map. Nine High-High counties form one block. They are Changsha, Wangcheng, Xiangtan, Zhuzhou, Miluo, Liuyang, Liling, Xiangyin and Shaoshan, the capital and the Changsha, Zhuzhou and Xiangtan area. title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
11.1 Deriving Distance Weight Matrix
Gi* is usually run with distance based weights. The book builds two kinds.

Computing fixed distance weightsComputing adaptive distance weights


critical_threshold() of sfdep finds the smallest distance at which every county has at least one neighbour.

ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(hunan))
ct

[1] 62954.89


st_dist_band() makes every county within that distance a neighbour. include_self() adds each county to its own neighbour list, and st_weights() row-standardises.

hunan_fdw <- hunan %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_dist_band(st_geometry(geometry), upper = ct)),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)



st_knn() of sfdep takes each county’s six nearest neighbours instead of a fixed radius.

hunan_adw <- hunan %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(st_knn(st_geometry(geometry), k = 6)),
         wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"),
         .before = 1)










NoteLearning diary



include_self() is what puts the star in Gi. The plain Gi statistic compares a county’s neighbours with the rest of the province and leaves the county out. Gi counts the county as part of its own neighbourhood. So one very rich county can make its own area a hot spot. This matters for Changsha, which is far richer than anything around it.
My cut-off is 63 km, against the book’s 60.8 km in zone 50. It also does not match Exercise 4, where the same UTM 49N projection with st_centroid() gave 58.3 km. The chunk below computes the cut-off from centroids and from st_point_on_surface() to see which point sfdep uses.



nn_cutoff <- function(pts) {
  xy <- st_coordinates(pts)
  max(unlist(nbdists(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = 1)), xy)))
}

round(c(centroid = nn_cutoff(st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan))),
        point_on_surface = nn_cutoff(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(hunan))),
        sfdep = ct))

        centroid point_on_surface            sfdep 
           58337            62955            62955 


The sfdep cut-off matches the point on surface version exactly. The centroid version gives the 58.3 km from Exercise 4. So sfdep measures from st_point_on_surface(), a point that always falls inside each polygon, not from the centroid. The difference between the two exercises came from the point used for each county, not from the projection.

11.6 Plotting and Visualising the HCSA Map
case_when() labels each county. Above 0.05 it is Insignificant. Otherwise it is a hot spot when Gi* is positive and a cold spot when Gi* is negative. I wrap the rule in classify_hcsa() because I use it again on the adaptive weights in Beyond the Exercise.

classify_hcsa <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(HCSA_cluster = case_when(
             p_sim > signif ~ "Insignificant",
             gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
             gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot"),
           HCSA_cluster = factor(HCSA_cluster,
                                 levels = c("Insignificant", "Hot spot", "Cold spot")),
           .before = 1)
}

HCSA_fdw <- classify_hcsa(HCSA_fdw)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
section: 12.1 Does Moran’s I Survive a Different Weights Matrix
text:
12.1 Does Moran’s I Survive a Different Weights Matrix
Exercise 4 ended with the point that the weights matrix is a choice I make. Every test above used Queen contiguity. Below I rerun moran.test() with four neighbour rules from that exercise, all row-standardised, to see whether the answer depends on the choice. The distance rules use the county centroids in UTM 49N and the cut-off ct from the hot spot section.

coords <- st_centroid(st_geometry(hunan))

w_list <- list(
  "Queen contiguity"     = nb2listw(poly2nb(hunan, queen = TRUE), style = "W"),
  "Rook contiguity"      = nb2listw(poly2nb(hunan, queen = FALSE), style = "W"),
  "Fixed distance"       = nb2listw(dnearneigh(coords, 0, ct),
                                    style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE),
  "Six nearest neighbours" = nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 6)),
                                      style = "W")
)

moran_by_w <- imap_dfr(w_list, function(lw, rule) {
  t <- moran.test(hunan$GDPPC, listw = lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
  tibble(`Neighbour rule` = rule,
         `Average neighbours` = round(mean(card(lw$neighbours)), 1),
         `Moran's I` = round(t$estimate[["Moran I statistic"]], 3),
         `Standard deviate` = round(t$statistic[[1]], 2),
         `p-value` = format.pval(t$p.value, digits = 2, eps = 1e-8))
})

kable(moran_by_w)
